title: India Just Launched Its First Mass-Market Ethanol Motorcycles. The Price Difference Is Less Than a Tank of Petrol.
excerpt: Hero MotoCorp's Splendor+ and HF Deluxe can now run on E85. With India importing 87% of its fossil fuel, the ₹172 premium on the cheapest model is a rounding error.
body:
Union Road Transport Minister Nitin Gadkari launched India's first mass-market flex-fuel motorcycles on Wednesday, putting ethanol-powered commuter bikes on the road at prices that barely register against their petrol-only counterparts. The Hero HF Deluxe Flex Fuel costs ₹72,792, just ₹172 more than the standard model. The Hero Splendor+ Flex Fuel comes in at ₹82,710, a premium of ₹2,479.

Both are capable of running on fuel blended with up to 85 percent ethanol, a first for motorcycles sold at scale in India. Deliveries begin July 26 in Delhi and Maharashtra, with a nationwide rollout to follow.

## Why this matters more than it looks

India imports 87 percent of its fossil fuel. That number, cited by Gadkari at the launch event, is the strategic context behind a pair of sub-₹1 lakh motorcycles that might otherwise seem like a footnote.

The Splendor and HF Deluxe families are not niche products. Together, they account for one in every three motorcycles on Indian roads. Hero MotoCorp sells millions of these bikes annually, overwhelmingly to commuters in smaller cities and rural areas where fuel costs are a meaningful share of household budgets. If flex-fuel variants capture even a fraction of that volume, the aggregate reduction in petrol consumption would be substantial.

The engineering changes are modest but deliberate. Both bikes use the same 97.2cc single-cylinder air-cooled engine as their standard counterparts, producing 8.57 PS and 8.3 Nm of torque — actually 7 percent more power than the regular models. Hero recalibrated the ECU, added a dedicated fuel pump designed for ethanol-rich blends, and installed a secondary fuel filter. The chassis, suspension, and braking hardware remain identical.

## The fuel infrastructure question

The practical constraint is not the motorcycle. It is the pump. India's ethanol blending programme has been scaling steadily — the country currently mandates E20 (20 percent ethanol blend) for regular petrol — but E85 fuel stations remain scarce. The initial launch in Delhi and Maharashtra reflects where the early infrastructure exists.

Gadkari addressed this directly, saying the government's focus is on expanding the E85 and E100 fuel network. He also dropped a signal that the flex-fuel push extends beyond two-wheelers: Maruti Suzuki is expected to launch India's first flex-fuel passenger car as early as this week.

## The ethanol economics

Ethanol in India is produced primarily from sugarcane and surplus foodgrains, which means fuel spending that currently flows to Middle Eastern oil producers would instead circulate through India's agricultural economy. At a moment when crude oil prices are near $96 a barrel — elevated by the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz disruptions — the case for reducing import dependence has rarely been more urgent.

Gadkari rejected the perception that ethanol is an inferior fuel. "These motorcycles can run on both petrol and ethanol. Ethanol is not an inferior fuel," he said, noting that technical evaluations show comparable power and torque.

## What it means for the diaspora

For NRIs who follow India's energy transition, the flex-fuel launch is a tangible step in a strategy that has mostly lived in policy documents. India's National Biofuels Policy targets 20 percent ethanol blending by 2025-26, and the E85 motorcycle is the clearest consumer-facing evidence that the target is translating into products.

The scale matters. If Hero MotoCorp rolls out flex-fuel variants across its lineup — and if the fuel infrastructure keeps pace — India could meaningfully reduce its oil import bill, which ran to over $150 billion last fiscal year. The Splendor Flex Fuel will not solve that problem alone. But at a ₹172 premium over the standard model, the barrier to adoption is effectively zero.

Hero developed both models at its Centre for Innovation and Technology in Jaipur. The flex-fuel technology has been engineered for Indian operating conditions, including high ambient temperatures and variable fuel quality. All fuel-contact components have been designed to withstand ethanol's different chemical properties for long-term reliability.
